title: Retention-constrained fine-tuning of a pre-trained aluminium MACE potential for non-equilibrium defect dynamics and plasticity
authors: Yue Wu, Yuan Tian, Deng Pan, Mingwei Chen
abstract: Adapting a pre-trained machine-learning interatomic potential for non-equilibrium defect dynamics and plasticity requires improving defect accuracy without degrading the near-equilibrium elastic and vibrational response. Here we achieve this balance for the aluminium MACE potential QP17 by integrating conditional readout uncertainty, iterative full-parameter updates and protocol-compatible relative-energy anchoring. Sensitivities over 144 linear readout weights guide acquisition, with within-batch covariance updates and evolving neural representations. After four active-learning rounds (32 acquired configurations and 400 gradient updates), force-uncertainty acquisition reduces mean development force error from 22.43 to 21.52 meV/Angstrom, outperforming random sampling (22.70), geometry-diversity selection (22.46) and uniform training across all 104 candidate labels (22.71) under the same update budget. All three force-uncertainty runs satisfy bulk-mechanical retention criteria: historical relative-energy error decreases from 0.375 to 0.207 meV/atom, while harmonic phonon root-mean-square drift remains below 0.05 THz. Matched objective ablations reveal that relative-energy anchoring suppresses harmonic drift. Out-of-sample evaluations across planar faults, twin boundaries and grain boundaries demonstrate transferable gains in defect energies and deviatoric stresses, even though virial stresses are never fitted. A closed-loop molecular dynamics and density functional theory (MD-DFT) pilot confirms that automated acceptance gating intercepts updates that violate historical elastic-group energy or vibrational tolerances. Together, these components establish a retention-constrained fine-tuning protocol for improving plastic-deformation observables while preserving the tested bulk mechanical response.

infographic.key_insight: Retention-constrained fine-tuning improves an aluminium MACE potential’s defect predictions while preserving tested near-equilibrium elastic and vibrational behavior.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The protocol supports more reliable atomistic simulations of plastic deformation without sacrificing validated bulk-mechanical response.
method: Select configurations using conditional force uncertainty, with within-batch covariance updates.
Iteratively update all model parameters while anchoring historical relative energies.
Gate updates against historical elastic-energy and vibrational tolerances.
infographic.evidence_signal: After 32 acquired configurations and 400 gradient updates, mean development force error fell from 22.43 to 21.52 meV/Å, outperforming sampling baselines; all three force-uncertainty runs met retention criteria, with harmonic phonon RMS drift below 0.05 THz.
infographic.watch_item: Retention is demonstrated only for the tested aluminium configurations and tolerances; broader deployment requires renewed validation and acceptance gating.
infographic.paper_title: Retention-constrained fine-tuning of a pre-trained aluminium MACE potential for non-equilibrium defect dynamics and plasticity

title: Constrained neural softening functions for the Mullins effect in parameter-dependent materials
authors: Dominik K. Klein, Jonas Fey, Maximilian Kannapinn, Oliver Weeger
abstract: Accurately capturing the Mullins effect across varying material compositions remains challenging, as constitutive models must unify flexible representations of stress softening with physical consistency and robust parameter calibration. In this work, we investigate parameter-dependent physics-augmented neural network constitutive models within the pseudo-elastic modeling framework, focusing on structural constraints that ensure physically admissible neural softening functions. This paper has three key contributions: (1) We formulate different neural softening functions within the pseudo-elastic framework, including a multiplicative decomposition of the softening function that enables parameter-dependent ansatz functions satisfying common mechanical constitutive conditions by construction. (2) We derive a sufficient condition for ellipticity of pseudo-elastic constitutive models, which can be enforced in the constitutive models by construction. (3) We systematically investigate how flexibility and structural constraints influence the performance of neural softening functions in terms of prediction accuracy and calibration robustness. For this, we consider multiaxial experimental data of carbon black-filled EPDM rubber synthesized with varying amounts of curatives. The findings of our work suggest that neural softening functions are a promising extension of the classical pseudo-elastic framework and, when subject to suitable constraints, can improve predictive accuracy for highly nonlinear, parameter-dependent materials.

infographic.key_insight: Structurally constrained neural softening functions extend pseudo-elastic Mullins models to capture composition-dependent stress softening while preserving physical admissibility.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could improve constitutive predictions and calibration reliability for rubber components with varying material formulations.
method: Embed parameter-dependent neural softening functions in a pseudo-elastic constitutive framework.
Use multiplicative softening decompositions to satisfy mechanical constraints by construction.
Derive an enforceable sufficient condition for ellipticity and assess flexibility–constraint trade-offs.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation uses multiaxial experimental data from carbon black-filled EPDM rubber with varying curative amounts to assess prediction accuracy and calibration robustness.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative performance gains or evidence of generalization beyond the studied EPDM formulations.
infographic.paper_title: Constrained neural softening functions for the Mullins effect in parameter-dependent materials

title: Universal neural network approximation of symmetric polyconvex energies and envelopes
authors: Florian Gammer
abstract: Symmetric polyconvexity provides a sufficient condition for weak lower semicontinuity in small-strain elasticity and a tractable lower bound for the relaxation of non-(quasi)convex energies. Since classical algorithms for computing such functions can be computationally expensive, neural network approximations have recently emerged as an alternative. A central difficulty with establishing such neural network based approaches for symmetric polyconvexity is the additional monotonicity property. As we show, the corresponding weight restrictions on ReLU-based input-convex networks do not yield universal approximation of the lifted representers. Here, we introduce symmetric polyconvex neural networks (SPCNNs) for constitutive modeling and approximation of symmetric polyconvex envelopes. The deep architecture combines convexity with the monotonicity required of a representer in the space of minors. We prove a universal approximation theorem for symmetric polyconvex energies, without requiring isotropy, and quantify the number of affine pieces attainable by the lifted network and derive reduced architectures for isotropic energies. Numerical examples illustrate stress-based regression and approximation of the symmetric polyconvex envelope of a double-well potential. Symmetric polyconvexity is guaranteed by construction, while the accuracy of the fitted energies and envelopes is assessed numerically.

infographic.key_insight: Symmetric polyconvex neural networks (SPCNNs) guarantee symmetric polyconvexity by construction and universally approximate symmetric polyconvex energies without requiring isotropy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: SPCNNs offer a structure-preserving approach to small-strain constitutive modeling and tractable lower bounds for relaxed nonconvex energies.
method: Combine convexity with the required monotonicity in a lifted space of minors.
Prove universal approximation and quantify attainable affine pieces.
Derive reduced architectures for isotropic energies.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical examples assess stress-based regression and approximation of the symmetric polyconvex envelope of a double-well potential.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy is assessed numerically; symmetric polyconvex envelopes provide lower bounds rather than necessarily the exact relaxed energy.
infographic.paper_title: Universal neural network approximation of symmetric polyconvex energies and envelopes

title: Microstructural Generative Inverse Models for Additive Manufacturing Digital Twins
authors: Pablo Luna Falcon, Jason Mayeur, Amirkoushyar Ziabari, Vincent Paquit, Patxi Fernandez-Zelaia
abstract: Metal additive manufacturing (AM) offers substantial advantages to the fabrication of complex structural components, but its widespread adoption is slowed due to complexities in the process-structure-property relations which is the cause for uncertainty and drives risk. Accurately quantifying these complex relations solely via experimental workflows is time consuming and costly. Integrated computational materials and engineering (ICME) frameworks address this challenge by leveraging advanced computational tools, such as crystal plasticity finite element models (CPFEM), to predict critical mechanical properties directly from microstructural data. However, these frameworks require a large datasets that are often difficult to obtain, and their predictive accuracy depends on the availability of realistic AM microstructure representations. Generative deep learning models are a promising approach towards synthesizing AM microstructures which contain complex morphological and crystallographic features. Denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs), in particular, show a strong potential to capture the inherent complexities of AM structures. In this work, we demonstrate that DDPMs can reliably synthesize digital-twin orientation-imaging micrographs, and we support this claim with quantitative evidence of the fidelity of the generated samples. Additionally, we establish a classifier-free guidance framework for solving complex inverse problems such as property-to-structure and process-to-structure mappings, and we showcase a potential application on a qualification-relevant uncertainty quantification problem. Our work highlights the potential of AI-based generative modeling as a key component of computational frameworks for accelerating AM materials qualification and certification.

infographic.key_insight: Denoising diffusion models generate realistic additive-manufacturing microstructure images and support inverse mappings from properties or process conditions to microstructure.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Synthetic microstructures could support crystal-plasticity simulations and uncertainty quantification for faster AM materials qualification.
method: Use denoising diffusion probabilistic models to synthesize orientation-imaging micrographs.
Apply classifier-free guidance to property-to-structure and process-to-structure inverse problems.
Demonstrate a qualification-relevant uncertainty quantification application.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports quantitative evidence of generated-sample fidelity but provides no dataset sizes, evaluation metrics, or numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Image fidelity alone does not establish accurate downstream mechanical predictions; simulation-based validation remains important.
infographic.paper_title: Microstructural Generative Inverse Models for Additive Manufacturing Digital Twins

title: Curvature-induced fracture mode coupling in doubly curved shells
authors: Riccardo Brambilla, Siddhant Kumar, Bianca Giovanardi
abstract: Classical shell fracture theories predominantly consider cracks aligned with principal curvature directions in cylindrical and spherical shells under tensile mode or pressure loading, leaving the fracture behavior of arbitrarily oriented cracks in doubly curved shells under general loading poorly understood. Here, we introduce a semi-analytical framework based on Reissner shallow-shell theory to investigate isotropic shells with positive, zero, and negative Gaussian curvature. The formulation computes stress intensity factors, energy release rates, and crack-lip displacements for arbitrarily inclined through-thickness cracks in spheres, ellipsoids, cylinders, hyperboloids, and minimal surfaces under general mechanical loading. We show that shell curvature couples opening, sliding, and tearing, allowing a single loading component to activate multiple fracture modes, unlike in flat plates. This coupling depends strongly on crack orientation and the normal, parallel, and torsional components of the shell curvature. Ellipsoids exhibit weak coupling, hyperboloids generally exhibit the strongest coupling, and cylinders display the most complex orientation-dependent responses. Moreover, in-plane shear can induce crack closure in hyperboloidal shells, suggesting a potential geometric mechanism for enhanced damage resistance. These findings elucidate the role of local curvature in fracture-mode coupling and provide a mechanistic foundation for the analysis of shellular (meta-)structures with engineered curvature distributions.

infographic.key_insight: Shell curvature couples crack opening, sliding, and tearing, so a single loading component can activate multiple fracture modes depending on crack orientation and local curvature.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Curvature-aware fracture analysis can inform damage-resistant shellular structures by accounting for geometry-driven mode coupling and possible crack closure.
method: Develop a semi-analytical framework using Reissner shallow-shell theory.
Analyze arbitrarily inclined through-thickness cracks in isotropic shells under general mechanical loading.
Compute stress intensity factors, energy release rates, and crack-lip displacements across multiple shell geometries.
infographic.evidence_signal: The reported analyses find weak coupling in ellipsoids, generally strongest coupling in hyperboloids, complex orientation-dependent responses in cylinders, and shear-induced crack closure in hyperboloidal shells.
infographic.watch_item: Applicability is bounded by shallow-shell and isotropic-material assumptions; the abstract does not report experimental validation.
infographic.paper_title: Curvature-induced fracture mode coupling in doubly curved shells

title: Evolution of microstructure and crystallographic texture in a novel Zr-4Nb-2Al alloy during hot rotary swaging
authors: Adam Strnad, Jana Šmilauerová, Josef Stráský, Lukáš Horák, Jan Čapek, Alžběta Endrychová
abstract: A multi-step induction-assisted hot rotary swaging route was developed for the novel dual-phase Zr-4Nb-2Al alloy to investigate the evolution of microstructure, crystallographic texture, and mechanical properties during sequential deformation. Phase-transformation temperatures determined by electrical resistivity measurements were used to select processing conditions in the single-phase $β$ field at 880°C and the $α+β$ field at 780°C. Induction heating with thermographic temperature control enabled reduction of the initial 12 mm rod to 6.3 mm, corresponding to a total area reduction of 72%. Swaging in the $β$ field refined millimetre-sized prior-$β$ grains to approximately 100 $μ$m, while subsequent cooling produced a fine lamellar $α+β$ microstructure. Further deformation in the $α+β$ field disrupted the lamellar structure, promoted globularisation and recrystallisation of the $α$ phase, and refined the $β$ phase. The microstructural evolution was accompanied by a pronounced $\langle 11\bar{2}0\rangle_α\parallel\mathrm{SD}$ fibre texture in the $α$ phase, whereas the $β$ phase exhibited predominantly $\langle 110\rangle_β\parallel\mathrm{SD}$ together with a $\langle 111\rangle_β\parallel\mathrm{SD}$ component. The phase constitution remained comparatively stable, with approximately 12-15 wt.% retained $β$ throughout processing. Subsequent $α+β$ swaging decreased the compressive yield strength from 1103 to 839 MPa while increasing plastic deformability, with a maximum fracture strain of 32%. Radial hardness heterogeneity was progressively eliminated. These results demonstrate that induction-assisted rotary swaging in selected phase fields provides an effective route for tailoring microstructure, texture, and mechanical response in dual-phase zirconium alloys.

infographic.key_insight: Sequential hot rotary swaging in the β and α+β phase fields refined Zr-4Nb-2Al microstructure and developed fibre textures, while subsequent α+β deformation traded compressive yield strength for greater plastic deformability.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Phase-field-controlled swaging offers a route to tailor strength, deformability, and radial hardness uniformity in dual-phase zirconium alloy rods.
method: Use electrical resistivity measurements to select β-field processing at 880°C and α+β processing at 780°C.
Apply induction-assisted rotary swaging with thermographic temperature control, reducing rod diameter from 12 to 6.3 mm.
Track microstructure, crystallographic texture, phase constitution, and mechanical response through sequential deformation.
infographic.evidence_signal: At 72% total area reduction, prior-β grains refined to approximately 100 µm; subsequent α+β swaging reduced compressive yield strength from 1103 to 839 MPa, with maximum fracture strain reaching 32%.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports compression performance only; tensile, fatigue, and service-environment behaviour remain unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Evolution of microstructure and crystallographic texture in a novel Zr-4Nb-2Al alloy during hot rotary swaging

title: An unconditionally convergent BDF2-type finite element integrator for the inertial Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation
authors: Michele Aldé, Hywel Normington, Dirk Praetorius, Michele Ruggeri
abstract: We propose and analyze a fully discrete numerical scheme to approximate solutions to the inertial Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert (iLLG) equation, a state-of-the-art model to describe the dynamics of the magnetization at subpicosecond time scales. The method employs first-order finite elements for the spatial discretization and the two-step backward differentiation formula (BDF2) for the time discretization, where the inertial term is treated by a convex combination of BDF2 and the backward Euler method. We prove well-posedness and unconditional stability of the scheme, and obtain explicit bounds for the error in the realization of the iLLG-inherent unit length constraint satisfied by the magnetization. Moreover, we derive the discrete energy law satisfied by the approximations, which resembles the inherent dissipative energy law of the model. Finally, with a constructive approach, we prove unconditional convergence of the approximations toward a weak solution of the problem. Numerical experiments assess the performance of the scheme and validate the theoretical findings.

infographic.key_insight: A BDF2-type finite element integrator for inertial magnetization dynamics is well-posed, unconditionally stable, and unconditionally convergent to a weak solution.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The scheme supports reliable simulation of subpicosecond magnetic dynamics without a stability-driven coupling between mesh size and time step.
method: Use first-order finite elements in space and BDF2 in time.
Treat inertia with a convex combination of BDF2 and backward Euler.
Establish a discrete dissipative energy law and explicit unit-length constraint error bounds.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical stability and convergence proofs, supported by numerical experiments assessing performance and validating the findings.
infographic.watch_item: Unconditional stability does not guarantee time-step-independent accuracy, and the magnetization's unit-length constraint is controlled by error bounds rather than enforced exactly.
infographic.paper_title: An unconditionally convergent BDF2-type finite element integrator for the inertial Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation

title: Robust augmented Block Preconditioning for two-phase Incompressible Inductionless MHD
authors: Bijie Song, Lingxiao Li, Jie Zhang
abstract: In this paper, we develop a robust augmented block preconditioner for three-dimensional, two-phase, incompressible inductionless MHD equations. We employ a high-order monolithic and charge-conservative arbitrary Lagrangian--Eulerian (ALE) finite element method as base scheme, for which the solution variables are current density, velocity, electric potential and pressure. Grad-div stabilization is added in both the current density equation and discrete momentum equation. Backward Euler method is used for the time discretization. At each time step, fully coupled solution strategy is adopted. This leads to large-scale, ill-conditioned, nonsymmetric, and indefinite dual saddle-point system. To solve this system efficiently, we construct an augmented block preconditioner within the constraint preconditioning framework. The ultimate preconditioner combines the augmented Lagrangian technique with approximate block factorization for current density sub-system and fluid sub-system. The fully coupled four-field system is then solved using preconditioned FGMRES iteration. Numerical experiments confirm the high-order accuracy and discrete charge conservation of the ALE-FEM. Drop of heavy fluid in light fluid is taken as benchmark to demonstrate the robustness of the preconditioner with respect to the discontinuity of physical parameters and the mesh size.

infographic.key_insight: An augmented block preconditioner enables robust iterative solution of fully coupled, three-dimensional, two-phase incompressible inductionless MHD systems.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports simulations of electrically conducting two-phase flows with discontinuous material properties and moving interfaces.
method: Discretize current density, velocity, electric potential and pressure using high-order, charge-conservative ALE finite elements and backward Euler time stepping.
Add grad-div stabilization to the current-density and momentum equations.
Combine augmented Lagrangian techniques with approximate block factorization, then solve the coupled system using preconditioned FGMRES.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments confirm high-order accuracy and discrete charge conservation; a heavy-fluid drop in a light fluid tests preconditioner robustness to material-property discontinuities and mesh size.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative iteration counts or timings, leaving practical computational gains and scalability unquantified.
infographic.paper_title: Robust augmented Block Preconditioning for two-phase Incompressible Inductionless MHD

title: Structure-preserving discretisations for the quasi-incompressible, thermal Maxwell-Stefan equations
authors: Boris D. Andrews, Aaron Baier-Reinio, Aaron Brunk, Patrick E. Farrell, Mária Lukáčová-Medviďová
abstract: We study a thermal Maxwell-Stefan-Navier-Stokes system modelling miscible mixtures under a quasi-incompressibility constraint. The system consists of the conservation laws for mass and momentum, and the balance law for entropy, which is preferred over the balance law for energy because it facilitates the development of two structure-preserving discretisation methods. The first method applies a semi-implicit Euler scheme in time, together with suitable finite elements in space, which guarantees generation of entropy and enforces the quasi-incompressibility constraint pointwise, but numerically dissipates total energy. The second method employs a continuous Petrov-Galerkin discretisation in time, which also generates entropy and satisfies the constraint pointwise, and in addition conserves the total energy and allows high-order time approximations. The structure-preserving properties and behaviour of both numerical methods are demonstrated by a series of numerical experiments.

infographic.key_insight: Two finite-element discretisations preserve entropy generation and pointwise quasi-incompressibility in thermal multicomponent flows, with the continuous Petrov–Galerkin method also conserving total energy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These methods support physically consistent simulation of miscible mixtures with coupled diffusion, heat transfer and fluid motion.
method: Formulate the thermal Maxwell–Stefan–Navier–Stokes system using an entropy balance.
Combine semi-implicit Euler time stepping with suitable finite elements; total energy is numerically dissipated.
Use continuous Petrov–Galerkin time discretisation to conserve total energy and enable high-order time approximations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments demonstrate the structure-preserving properties and behaviour of both methods, but the abstract provides no quantitative error or runtime results.
infographic.watch_item: The semi-implicit Euler method introduces numerical energy dissipation, which may matter when energy conservation is critical.
infographic.paper_title: Structure-preserving discretisations for the quasi-incompressible, thermal Maxwell-Stefan equations

title: MarkovSim: an LLM Agent Harness with Bounded Context for Long-Horizon Computational Simulation
authors: Yeui-Lung Lei, Wen-Bo Chen, Pan Zhang
abstract: Recent studies have applied large language model (LLM) agent systems to computational simulation workflows. Such workflows are long-horizon, so the information generated can exceed what an LLM can reason over at once, its context window. Context management is therefore essential, yet existing systems have either neglected it or treated it as a supporting mechanism rather than a subject of study. This paper presents MarkovSim, an LLM agent harness for long-horizon computational simulation, whose core is a context management scheme built into the workflow. The workflow record is written to a memory system with a predefined schema, and at workflow-defined boundaries, namely the state transitions of a finite-state machine a compact representation of the solution progress is constructed from it as the agent's context. Instantiated on finite element analysis and evaluated on six benchmark problems, MarkovSim passed 16 of 18 runs and corrected its own faults in both the solver operations and the model physics. The engineer was consulted only where engineering judgement was needed. The context remained bounded throughout every run, regardless of its length.

infographic.key_insight: MarkovSim keeps LLM context bounded during long-horizon simulation by rebuilding compact progress summaries at finite-state workflow transitions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For finite element analysis, the harness supports automated workflows and fault correction while reserving engineering judgment for human consultation.
method: Store workflow records in schema-defined memory.
Organize simulation tasks with a finite-state machine.
Construct compact agent context from memory at state transitions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across six finite element benchmark problems, MarkovSim passed 16 of 18 runs, corrected solver-operation and model-physics faults, and maintained bounded context in every run.
infographic.watch_item: The six-problem evaluation leaves generalization to broader simulation tasks and the reliability of compact context summaries unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: MarkovSim: an LLM Agent Harness with Bounded Context for Long-Horizon Computational Simulation

title: Clustering Templates: A Data-Driven Framework for Dimensionality Reduction and Compression of Brain Strain in Head Impact
authors: Junxi Liu, Xiaoyu Du, Jingyi Wu, Yang Wang, Chongmin Zhang, Yihan Zhang
abstract: Purpose: Finite element (FE) models are indispensable for studying the biomechanics of traumatic brain injury (TBI), and modern head FE models typically comprise thousands to millions of elements. The resulting brain strain is therefore high-dimensional, and when combined with dense temporal sampling and large numbers of head impact cases, this produces datasets of substantial data volume. Accordingly, this study investigates the effective dimensionality required to accurately represent brain strain and proposes a data-driven framework to reduce the dimensionality of FE simulation data while maintaining high spatiotemporal fidelity. Methods: We developed a series of "clustering templates" by applying K-means clustering to feature vectors derived from the maximum principal strain (MPS) time-history curves of 118,840 brain elements over 3,693 impact simulations using the THUMS head model. The performance of these templates, with cluster counts (K) ranging from 8 to 8192, was rigorously evaluated by quantifying the fidelity of data reconstruction. Results: The clustering templates demonstrated high-fidelity reconstruction of the original FE data. A template with K = 512 achieved a compression ratio of over 200:1 while maintaining a low mean element-wise peak MPS root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.027, and a template with K = 4096 (30:1 compression ratio) achieved an RMSE of 0.016. Conclusion: The proposed clustering templates provide an effective and automated method for the dimensionality reduction and compression of large-scale brain strain data. This framework mitigates critical data management bottlenecks and enables the development of subsequent data analysis and machine learning models, thereby accelerating research in TBI biomechanics.

infographic.key_insight: Clustering brain elements by their strain histories enables over 200:1 compression while retaining high-fidelity representations of simulated brain strain.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Compact strain representations reduce storage burdens and support downstream analysis and machine learning for traumatic brain injury biomechanics.
method: Extract features from element-wise maximum principal strain (MPS) time histories.
Apply K-means to build clustering templates with 8–8192 clusters.
Evaluate reconstruction fidelity against the original finite element strain data.
infographic.evidence_signal: Using 3,693 THUMS impact simulations with 118,840 brain elements, K = 512 achieved over 200:1 compression with mean element-wise peak MPS RMSE of 0.027; K = 4096 achieved 30:1 compression with RMSE of 0.016.
infographic.watch_item: Transferability to other head models or impact conditions is not established by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Clustering Templates: A Data-Driven Framework for Dimensionality Reduction and Compression of Brain Strain in Head Impact

title: Reliability Assessment of FRP-RC Columns Using AK-MCS with a Piecewise Two-Branch Approach
authors: Arndt Goldack, Richard Koehler, Ahmed Usama Syed
abstract: Slender concrete columns reinforced with fiber-reinforced polymer (FRP) bars fail at medium to high axial load levels either by concrete crushing or by loss of stability, while the tensile strains in the reinforcement remain far below the rupture strain. Each non-linear finite element (FE) analysis yields only the capacity of the governing failure mode, and the governing mode changes over a broad zone in which both capacities are nearly equal. Both characteristics conflict with active-learning Kriging-assisted Monte Carlo simulation (AK-MCS), which assumes a single, smooth limit-state function. This paper proposes a piecewise, two-branch AK-MCS framework in which each failure mode is represented by its own Kriging model, trained only on the FE analyses in which that mode governs, and the governing prediction is the minimum of both. Safeguards against data starvation keep rarely governing branches usable. After convergence, additional FE analyses are placed based on a leave-one-out calibration check and on the width of the confidence interval on the reliability index. A design-point search on the surrogate and importance sampling at the design points provide the reliability index even where direct Monte Carlo simulation finds no failure. For an FRP-reinforced concrete column example with mixed failure, 79% and 62% of the training points lie near the mode boundary. The reliability index from the design-point search agrees with the Monte Carlo estimate to within 0.05, and an FE analysis at the design point confirms the surrogate to within 0.6%.

infographic.key_insight: Separate Kriging surrogates for concrete crushing and instability enable reliability assessment of FRP-reinforced concrete columns when the governing failure mode switches.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports reliability estimation for slender FRP-RC columns, including rare-failure cases where direct Monte Carlo simulation detects no failures.
method: Train one Kriging model per failure mode using only FE analyses where that mode governs, then take the minimum prediction.
Use active learning, data-starvation safeguards, and post-convergence refinement guided by leave-one-out calibration and reliability-index uncertainty.
Search for surrogate design points and perform importance sampling around them.
infographic.evidence_signal: In the mixed-failure column example, reported training-point concentrations near the mode boundary were 79% and 62%; design-point and Monte Carlo reliability indices differed by at most 0.05, and FE verification at the design point agreed within 0.6%.
infographic.watch_item: Rarely governing failure modes can lack training data, making branch-specific safeguards and FE validation important.
infographic.paper_title: Reliability Assessment of FRP-RC Columns Using AK-MCS with a Piecewise Two-Branch Approach

title: A van der Waals Floating-Gate Platform for Broadband Optoelectronic Neuromorphic Computing
authors: Thi Phuong Anh Bach, Sangeun Cho
abstract: Artificial synapses that integrate nonvolatile memory with broadband optoelectronic learning are essential for next-generation neuromorphic computing. However, their realization remains challenging because conventional floating-gate memories exhibit limited optical functionality and poor scalability. Here, we report a van der Waals ReS2/hBN/InSe floating-gate synaptic transistor that combines efficient charge storage with broadband optoelectronic learning in a single device architecture. The heterostructure incorporates InSe as a floating-gate layer for stable charge storage, hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) as a tunneling dielectric, and ReS2 as a photoresponsive channel, enabling carrier tunneling under electrical and optical stimulation. Through the combined operation of these layers, the device achieves a large memory window, an on/off current ratio exceeding 10^6, stable multilevel conductance states, and reliable retention over 10^4 s. Broadband visible-to-near-infrared optical excitation enables controllable synaptic weight modulation and the emulation of essential synaptic functions, including short- and long-term plasticity, paired-pulse facilitation, and pulse-amplitude- and pulse-duration-dependent plasticity. Optical potentiation and electrical depression further enable bidirectional modulation of synaptic weights. Beyond these synaptic functions, the device demonstrates higher-order learning through associative and discrimination conditioning inspired by the Pavlovian learning paradigm, as well as reconfigurable Boolean logic driven by electro-optical inputs. These results establish a multifunctional van der Waals floating-gate platform that integrates nonvolatile memory, broadband optoelectronic learning, and adaptive information processing within a single transistor, providing a promising strategy for compact, energy-efficient neuromorphic hardware.

infographic.key_insight: A ReS2/hBN/InSe van der Waals floating-gate transistor integrates nonvolatile memory, broadband optoelectronic synaptic learning, and adaptive logic in one device.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The platform could support compact neuromorphic hardware that combines optical sensing, memory, and information processing.
method: Stack a photoresponsive ReS2 channel, hBN tunneling dielectric, and InSe floating gate.
Modulate stored charge and synaptic conductance using visible-to-near-infrared light and electrical pulses.
Demonstrate synaptic plasticity, Pavlovian-inspired conditioning, and reconfigurable Boolean logic.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports an on/off current ratio exceeding 10^6, stable multilevel conductance, retention over 10^4 s, and bidirectional optical potentiation/electrical depression.
infographic.watch_item: Array-scale integration, device variability, endurance, and energy per operation are not established in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: A van der Waals Floating-Gate Platform for Broadband Optoelectronic Neuromorphic Computing

title: A Two-Grid Finite Element Method for the Nonlinear Poisson-Boltzmann Equation Based on a Solution Decomposition
authors: Zhen Chao, Jingchun Chen, Cong He
abstract: The nonlinear Poisson--Boltzmann equation (PBE) is a widely used implicit-solvent model for the electrostatics of biomolecules in ionic solvent. Its numerical solution is complicated by the point charges, the dielectric jump across the molecular surface, and the exponential nonlinearity. We study a two-grid finite element method for the PBE built on the solution decomposition $u=G+Ψ+\Phit$ of Xie [J.~Comput.~Phys.~275 (2014) 294--309], in which $G$ carries the singularities analytically, $Ψ$ solves a linear interface problem, and $\Phit$ solves a semilinear interface problem for an arbitrary number of ionic species. The nonlinear problem for $\Phit$ is solved on a coarse mesh only, followed by a single Newton correction on the fine mesh, so that only symmetric positive definite linear systems are solved on the fine mesh. The analysis uses a $C^2$ truncation of the exponential that grows quadratically beyond a level $τ$; for $τ$ above an explicit bound the truncated problem has the same solution as the original one, and no discrete maximum principle or mesh-angle condition is needed. Under standard piecewise regularity assumptions we prove quasi-optimal energy and $L^2$ estimates and an $L^4$ estimate for the finite element approximation of $\Phit$, and for the two-grid solution we prove $\enorm{u-\utg}\le C\big(h^{s-1}+H^{2(s-1)+t/2}\big)$ in three dimensions, where $t=\min\{s,σ\}-1$. Whenever the dual problem is at least as regular as the primal one ($σ\ge s$), the coarse mesh can be chosen as $H\sim h^{2/5}$ without loss of accuracy. A manufactured-solution test confirms the predicted rates and the quadratic dependence of the two-grid correction on the coarse error.

infographic.key_insight: A two-grid finite element method moves nonlinear Poisson–Boltzmann solves to a coarse mesh while retaining fine-mesh accuracy through one Newton correction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach reduces fine-mesh nonlinear computation for biomolecular electrostatics with singular charges and discontinuous dielectric properties.
method: Decompose the potential into analytic charge singularities, a linear interface solution, and a semilinear interface solution.
Solve the semilinear problem on a coarse mesh, then apply one fine-mesh Newton correction using symmetric positive definite linear systems.
Use a C² exponential truncation for analysis without requiring a discrete maximum principle or mesh-angle condition.
infographic.evidence_signal: A manufactured-solution test confirms predicted convergence rates and quadratic dependence of the two-grid correction error on the coarse-grid error.
infographic.watch_item: The accuracy-preserving choice H ∼ h^(2/5) requires the dual problem to be at least as regular as the primal problem; evidence reported here is limited to a manufactured test.
infographic.paper_title: A Two-Grid Finite Element Method for the Nonlinear Poisson-Boltzmann Equation Based on a Solution Decomposition

title: A Gaussian Process State Space Formulation for Materials Constitutive Modeling: Application to Quasi-brittle Materials
authors: Houlin Xu, Chenyang Li, K. T. Ramesh, Michael D. Shields
abstract: Constitutive models for history-dependent, path-dependent materials typically encode this dependence in prescribed functional forms through internal variables such as damage or plastic strain that are phenomenological, model-dependent, and not directly observable. These rigid forms lack flexibility to match observations, make calibration potentially non-unique, and complicate uncertainty quantification. This paper develops a Gaussian-process state-space model (GP-SSM) that replaces the fixed form of the constitutive model with a flexible GP regression, and the prescribed internal variables with latent state variables learned directly from observable stress-strain histories. As a GP, the model is naturally endowed with a measure of uncertainty and can be constrained to satisfy physical principles. We demonstrate this framework for quasi-brittle materials under triaxial compression, where the latent variable evolution is driven by the current-state stress invariants and the increment of equivalent strain to reflect irreversible, pressure-sensitive history. A sparse multi-output GP then maps the latent state and current strain tensor to the six-component stress response, trained by variational sparse inference. The trained model is exported into Abaqus/Explicit through a user material subroutine. Four verification cases are reported: (1) offline rollout on validation and test histories; (2) a single element under changing confinement; (3) a frozen-memory unloading-reloading extension; and (4) a multi-element structural model compared against the Karagozian and Case Concrete (KCC) model. These results show that the learned state-space update reproduces held-out RVE-scale histories in closed-loop rollout, tracks evolving confinement, supports unloading without violating the irreversibility of the learned history state, and reproduces structural-level behavior consistent with KCC.

infographic.key_insight: A Gaussian-process state-space model learns latent material memory directly from stress–strain histories, replacing prescribed constitutive forms and internal variables.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Integration into Abaqus/Explicit enables finite-element simulation of history-dependent, pressure-sensitive quasi-brittle materials with GP-based uncertainty estimates.
method: Evolve latent history states using current stress invariants and equivalent-strain increments.
Map latent states and current strain to six-component stress using a sparse multi-output GP trained by variational inference.
Export the learned constitutive update through an Abaqus/Explicit user material subroutine.
infographic.evidence_signal: Four verification cases assess held-out history rollouts, changing confinement, frozen-memory unloading–reloading, and multi-element structural response consistent with KCC.
infographic.watch_item: The reported checks do not establish reliability beyond the evaluated loading paths; unloading–reloading uses a frozen-memory extension.
infographic.paper_title: A Gaussian Process State Space Formulation for Materials Constitutive Modeling: Application to Quasi-brittle Materials

title: Facet normals of Minkowski sums of staircase simplices
authors: Yushan Qu, Jon Lee
abstract: Staircase simplices are the simplices of the standard (Freudenthal--Kuhn) triangulation of $[0,1]^d$ and of Stanley's triangulations of order polytopes. We study the facet normals of their Minkowski sums and how the number of summands constrains the size of primitive integer normals. We characterize the normals attainable with a prescribed number of summands in terms of $d-1$ linearly independent zero-one vectors orthogonal to the normal, whose supports have an intersection graph that can be colored with one color per summand. This gives a combinatorial characterization of the least number of summands needed to realize a normal. For two summands, all primitive normals have entries in $\{-1,0,1\}$, and we determine which of them occur. For three summands we bound every entry in absolute value by $3^{(d-2)/3}$ and construct normals with entries of order $θ^d$, $θ$ the plastic number; for four summands a second construction gives entries of order $ψ^d$, $ψ$ the supergolden ratio. Since $ψ>3^{1/3}$, the largest coefficients for three and four summands are exponentially separated. For vectors with at most two distinct nonzero entry values, we determine the least number of summands exactly, using a matching-rank formula proved by exterior algebra and representations of symmetric groups. With no restriction on the number of summands, the maximum coefficient equals the classical maximum for facets of $0/1$-polytopes in the same dimension.

infographic.key_insight: The number of staircase simplices in a Minkowski sum controls its primitive facet-normal coefficients, with exponentially larger coefficients attainable for four summands than for three.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These results may inform exact polyhedral geometry algorithms by clarifying how Minkowski-sum complexity affects integer coefficient sizes.
method: Characterize attainable normals using d−1 independent orthogonal zero-one vectors and colorings of their support-intersection graph.
Derive coefficient bounds and exponential-growth constructions for fixed numbers of summands.
Determine minimum summand counts for normals with at most two distinct nonzero values using a matching-rank formula.
infographic.evidence_signal: The evidence is theoretical: two summands permit only coefficients in {−1,0,1}, three satisfy the bound 3^((d−2)/3), and four admit growth exceeding that exponential rate.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports no computational benchmarks or solid-mechanics validation, so practical performance and application benefits remain untested.
infographic.paper_title: Facet normals of Minkowski sums of staircase simplices

title: Synthetic Deformable Tubular Benchmark: A mechanically annotated dataset for evaluating deformable 3D reconstruction
authors: Íñigo Cirauqui-Viloria
abstract: Evaluating deformable 3D reconstruction requires ground truth linking camera motion, surface deformation, material correspondence and image appearance. We introduce the Synthetic Deformable Tubular Benchmark, generated with LumenMorph, an open-source toolkit for creating, annotating and evaluating tubular scenes. The release contains 5,580 RGB images. Its baseline crosses three surface-motion conditions with moving and stationary cameras in six scene families; matched appearance variants cover only moving-camera finite-element actions in four families. Documented public and evaluation interfaces expose camera poses, geometry, depth, deformation fields, persistent material correspondences and discrete finite-element records. Persistent triangle identities and material weights let users track the same surface location across frames and query its three-dimensional trajectory. Separately implemented geometric and mechanical checks assess annotation consistency with the generating models. Structure-from-motion, optical-flow and supplied-geometry displacement-interpolation studies demonstrate how the resource distinguishes registration coverage from geometric accuracy, exposes camera- and surface-motion effects, and tests the benefits and mismatch of mechanical priors. Public readers, evaluation contracts and the configurable generator support reuse and extension. Data integrity, fixed-environment repeatability and retained-prediction score replay have distinct verification scopes. The benchmark provides a controlled synthetic reference without claiming anatomical or clinical realism.

infographic.key_insight: The Synthetic Deformable Tubular Benchmark links image appearance, camera motion and surface mechanics to evaluate deformable 3D reconstruction with persistent material correspondence.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It supports controlled testing of reconstruction and displacement-estimation methods under camera motion, surface deformation and mechanical-prior mismatch.
method: Generate and annotate tubular scenes with the open-source LumenMorph toolkit.
Cross three surface-motion conditions with moving and stationary cameras across six baseline scene families.
Track material points using persistent triangle identities and weights, with separate geometric and mechanical consistency checks.
infographic.evidence_signal: The release contains 5,580 RGB images and includes structure-from-motion, optical-flow and supplied-geometry displacement-interpolation studies that distinguish registration coverage from geometric accuracy.
infographic.watch_item: The benchmark is synthetic and does not claim anatomical or clinical realism; matched appearance variants cover only moving-camera finite-element actions in four families.
infographic.paper_title: Synthetic Deformable Tubular Benchmark: A mechanically annotated dataset for evaluating deformable 3D reconstruction

title: One-Sided $p$-Explicit Stability for High-Order Cut Finite Element Nitsche Methods
authors: Erik Burman, Peter Hansbo, Mats G. Larson, Karl Larsson
abstract: We give a one-sided stability argument for high-order cut finite elements with symmetric Nitsche boundary conditions. On each boundary patch, an $H^1$-projection splits the discrete function into a single polynomial and a stabilized residual. Inward segments control the polynomial inside the physical domain; complete-element estimates control only the residual. For smooth exterior boundaries and under a geometry-dependent mesh restriction, this gives an explicit normal-flux estimate with factor $p^2/h$ and a sufficient Nitsche penalty with the same scaling. The constants are independent of the cut position and polynomial degree. A neighboring-interval estimate quantifies the exponential cost of polynomial continuation and motivates avoiding it in the stability proof. We obtain $hp$-error estimates, with half a power of degree lost in energy and a full power in $L^2$ relative to best approximation, and exponential degree convergence for analytic extensions on sufficiently fine meshes. Translated-disk experiments show bounded normalized flux constants and penalty thresholds over the tested degrees and cuts, and resolved convergence curves follow the predicted orders. Physical and extension-dependent stabilization errors are reported separately.

infographic.key_insight: A one-sided stability argument yields cut-position- and degree-independent constants with explicit p²/h scaling for normal-flux control and a sufficient Nitsche penalty.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The result supports stable high-order finite element analysis on unfitted meshes without requiring the mesh to conform to smooth exterior boundaries.
method: Use a patchwise H¹ projection to split the discrete solution into a polynomial and a stabilized residual.
Control the polynomial along inward segments in the physical domain and the residual on complete elements.
Avoid exponentially costly polynomial continuation and derive hp-error estimates.
infographic.evidence_signal: Translated-disk experiments show bounded normalized flux constants and penalty thresholds over tested degrees and cuts, with resolved convergence curves following predicted orders.
infographic.watch_item: The theory requires smooth exterior boundaries and a geometry-dependent mesh restriction, and loses half a degree power in energy error and a full power in L² error relative to best approximation.
infographic.paper_title: One-Sided $p$-Explicit Stability for High-Order Cut Finite Element Nitsche Methods

title: A Differentiable Framework for Inverse Identification of Heterogeneous Cohesive Laws
authors: Sida Hao, Jinkyo Han, Bahador Bahmani
abstract: This work develops a differentiable finite element framework based on an intrinsic cohesive-zone formulation for identifying traction-separation laws from global force-displacement histories and spatially sparse strain measurements. The framework employs physics-constrained neural networks to represent flexible, thermodynamically structured cohesive laws, with sensitivities computed through automatic differentiation and a discrete adjoint that accounts for the history-dependent evolution of interfacial damage. To enable identification of spatially heterogeneous cohesive behavior, we extend learned constitutive priors to irreversible interfacial damage by constructing a shared, low-dimensional family of cohesive laws from representative traction-separation histories. This representation exploits common constitutive structure and parameter sharing to reduce the number of unknowns and regularize the inverse problem, while allowing local cohesive behavior to vary spatially through latent coordinates. Numerical investigations involving double-cantilever beams and fiber-matrix composites demonstrate that accurate reproduction of global force-displacement responses does not necessarily imply accurate recovery of the underlying cohesive laws. Incorporating spatially resolved strain measurements substantially improves constitutive identification, even when the admissible responses are constrained by a learned prior. Comparisons with conventional bilinear cohesive models and Bayesian optimization further illustrate the benefits of the learned constitutive representation and adjoint-based identification for high-dimensional inverse problems.

infographic.key_insight: Matching global force–displacement curves alone can conceal incorrect cohesive laws; spatial strain measurements substantially improve their identification.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports identification of spatially varying interface damage laws relevant to delamination and fiber–matrix debonding.
method: Represent cohesive laws with thermodynamically structured, physics-constrained neural networks in an intrinsic cohesive-zone finite element model.
Compute sensitivities using automatic differentiation and a discrete adjoint that accounts for damage history.
Regularize heterogeneous identification with a shared, low-dimensional learned prior and spatially varying latent coordinates.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical studies of double-cantilever beams and fiber–matrix composites evaluate constitutive recovery, including comparisons with bilinear cohesive models and Bayesian optimization.
infographic.watch_item: The evidence is numerical; reliable identification still depends on informative spatial strain measurements, even with a learned prior.
infographic.paper_title: A Differentiable Framework for Inverse Identification of Heterogeneous Cohesive Laws

title: Entropic Control for Homeostatic Optimization: Pre-empting Catastrophic Forgetting via Dynamic Feedback
authors: Shangxi Wu, Xiaorong Yan, Xiaojun Meng, Yuxiang Zhang, Jiansheng Wei
abstract: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) of LLMs suffers from catastrophic forgetting, and prevailing mitigation strategies struggle to reconcile the plasticity-stability dilemma. To address this, we propose Entropic Control for Homeostatic Optimization (ECHO), a closed-loop control framework. By decomposing the KL divergence, we identify output entropy as a dominant observable component of KL variation. This enables us to leverage entropy as a computationally efficient online proxy to monitor forgetting risks in real-time, bypassing expensive reference-model inference. Consequently, ECHO employs an elastic controller that dynamically modulates the gradient weight of replay data via a proportional control law, using deviations from the pre-trained entropic equilibrium as an error signal. Empirical evaluations across 0.6B to 9B parameter architectures demonstrate that ECHO lies on, and in several comparisons extends, the observed plasticity-stability frontier and maintains high operational robustness against varying data mixing ratios.

infographic.key_insight: ECHO uses output-entropy feedback to dynamically adjust replay-gradient weighting and mitigate catastrophic forgetting during LLM supervised fine-tuning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach may help preserve general capabilities when adapting engineering language models, but the abstract reports no solid-mechanics or constitutive-modeling validation.
method: Use KL-divergence decomposition to motivate output entropy as an online proxy for forgetting risk.
Measure deviations from the pre-trained model’s entropic equilibrium without reference-model inference.
Apply proportional feedback to dynamically modulate replay-data gradient weight.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluations on 0.6B–9B parameter architectures reportedly match or extend the observed plasticity–stability frontier in several comparisons and remain robust across varying data-mixing ratios.
infographic.watch_item: Entropy is a proxy rather than a direct measure of retained knowledge; its reliability and controller tuning require validation for each target domain.
infographic.paper_title: Entropic Control for Homeostatic Optimization: Pre-empting Catastrophic Forgetting via Dynamic Feedback
